front: What is noise-trader risk in the De Long, Shleifer, Summers & Waldmann (DSSW 1990) framework?
back: Noise-trader risk is the risk that irrational investor sentiment worsens in the short run, driving asset prices even further away from fundamental value before fundamentals can reassert themselves. Because rational arbitrageurs have finite investment horizons and risk aversion, this resale-price risk limits their willingness to take aggressive contrarian positions.

front: How does the DSSW (1990) model overturn Milton Friedman's (1953) classic market selection hypothesis?
back: Friedman argued irrational traders lose money to rational arbitrageurs and are driven from the market. DSSW prove noise traders can earn higher average returns than rational investors ('create their own space') because their misperception leads them to hold more of the risky asset, bearing more of their own self-created resale-price risk and earning a positive risk premium in equilibrium.

front: What are the four components of the equilibrium asset price in the DSSW (1990) OLG model?
back: The equilibrium price decomposes into: (1) fundamental value V = d/r; (2) the average sentiment price markup (mu * mu_rho)/r; (3) the resale price risk discount -(2 * gamma * mu^2 * sigma_rho^2)/(r * (1+r)^2); and (4) the transitory sentiment fluctuation shock mu*(rho_t - mu_rho)/(1+r).

front: Why does performance-based arbitrage (Shleifer & Vishny 1997) exacerbate rather than eliminate mispricings during liquidity crises?
back: Professional arbitrageurs manage outside client capital. When negative sentiment shocks widen a mispricing, fund portfolios show paper losses. Uninformed investors interpret losses as poor manager skill and withdraw capital precisely at the trough, forcing fund managers to liquidate positions into falling markets and widening the dislocation.

front: How do fundamental risk and noise-trader risk differ as limits to arbitrage?
back: Fundamental risk is the risk that asset cash flows or intrinsic values change adversely (e.g. unexpected firm bankruptcy). Noise-trader risk exists even when fundamental cash flows are perfectly deterministic and known: it is the risk that other investors' irrational beliefs become more extreme at the arbitrageur's liquidation horizon.

front: What is the 'hold more space' effect in behavioral asset pricing?
back: The phenomenon whereby bullish noise traders systematically allocate a larger fraction of their wealth to risky assets than rational arbitrageurs. If the risky asset earns an equity risk premium on average, noise traders accumulate wealth faster in expectation despite sub-optimal market timing.

front: What empirical pattern did De Bondt & Thaler (1985) discover regarding long-term stock returns?
back: Over 3- to 5-year evaluation windows, past long-term losers (worst performing decile) significantly outperform past long-term winners by approximately 25-30% cumulative excess return, providing early empirical evidence of stock market overreaction to persistent past corporate earnings trends.

front: How does the Barberis, Shleifer & Vishny (BSV 1998) model generate both underreaction and overreaction?
back: Investors believe corporate earnings alternate between two unobservable Markov regimes: a mean-reverting regime (conservatism heuristic, causing underreaction to single earnings surprises) and a trending regime (representativeness heuristic, causing overreaction when a firm reports consecutive earnings increases).

front: What cognitive mechanisms drive asset pricing dynamics in Daniel, Hirshleifer & Subrahmanyam (DHS 1998)?
back: Investor overconfidence in the precision of private signals (which creates initial overreaction) combined with biased self-attribution (confirming public news boosts confidence while disconfirming news is dismissed as bad luck, amplifying mispricing in the intermediate term before fundamental reality forces reversal).

front: In the Hong & Stein (1999) unified model, what role do 'news watchers' play?
back: News watchers form forecasts based on private fundamental information, but information diffuses gradually across the population of news watchers at speed z. Because news is absorbed slowly into prices, news watchers alone generate price underreaction and positive short-run return momentum.

front: Why do 'momentum traders' in Hong & Stein (1999) inevitably cause long-run price overreaction?
back: Momentum traders condition only on past price changes and pursue trend-following strategies over lookback horizon j. While trend-chasing initially accelerates price adjustment toward fundamentals, momentum traders continue buying after price has reached intrinsic value, creating endogenous overshooting and eventual reversals.

front: How do short-run momentum and long-run reversal reconcile across evaluation horizons?
back: Short-run momentum (3-12 months, Jegadeesh & Titman 1993) reflects initial underreaction to information diffusion or self-attribution feedback, while long-run reversal (3-5 years, De Bondt & Thaler 1985) reflects the subsequent correction of accumulated overreaction.

front: What is an investor sentiment index in the Baker & Wurgler (2006) framework?
back: A composite time-series index extracted as the first principal component of multiple market-wide sentiment proxies, orthogonalized with respect to macroeconomic business-cycle variables to isolate irrational investor optimism or pessimism from fundamental economic state variation.

front: Which six empirical proxies comprise the Baker & Wurgler (2006) investor sentiment index?
back: The six proxies are: (1) the closed-end fund discount (CEFD); (2) detrended NYSE share turnover (TURN); (3) number of IPOs (NIPO); (4) first-day average IPO return (RIPO); (5) equity share in total new equity and debt issues (S); and (6) the dividend premium (PDND, price difference between dividend payers and non-payers).

front: Why does Baker & Wurgler sentiment affect the cross-section of stock returns asymmetrically?
back: Stocks differ along two key dimensions: subjectivity of valuation (hard vs easy to value) and limits to arbitrage (cost of shorting, idiosyncratic risk). Speculative, young, unprofitable, high-volatility, and growth firms have no objective cash-flow anchors and face severe short-sale constraints, making them disproportionately sensitive to sentiment shifts.

front: What does high investor sentiment predict for subsequent cross-sectional stock returns?
back: High sentiment predicts significantly low subsequent returns for speculative, young, small, and high-volatility stocks relative to safe, mature, dividend-paying stocks. When sentiment is low, this spread reverses: speculative stocks earn higher subsequent returns than safe stocks.

front: Why must sentiment proxies be orthogonalized against macroeconomic indicators before principal component extraction?
back: Raw proxies contain both irrational sentiment and rational business-cycle responses (e.g. IPO activity rises in economic booms due to lower cost of capital). Regressing proxies on macroeconomic variables (IP growth, consumption, term and default spreads) strips out rational macro variation, isolating pure behavioral sentiment.

front: What is the Greenwood & Shleifer (2014) empirical puzzle regarding survey expectations of stock returns?
back: Across six independent surveys of retail and institutional investors, survey expected returns are strongly positively correlated with past stock returns and current valuation multiples (price-dividend ratios), directly contradicting rational discount-rate asset pricing models where high valuations imply low future expected returns.

front: What is the empirical correlation between survey expected returns and rational realized stock returns?
back: Greenwood & Shleifer (2014) find that survey expectations of stock returns are negatively correlated with subsequent realized market excess returns (and negatively correlated with rational expected returns implied by consumption-based or present-value models).

front: How are extrapolative expectations formalized mathematically?
back: Extrapolative expectations model subjective return expectations as an exponentially weighted moving average of past realized returns: E_t^e[R_{t+1}] = (1 - theta) * sum_{k=0}^infty theta^k * R_{t-k}, where 0 < theta < 1 determines the memory weighting of recent price changes.

front: How do Bordalo, Gennaioli, La Porta & Shleifer (2019) define diagnostic expectations?
back: Diagnostic expectations formalize Kahneman and Tversky's representativeness heuristic as a probability belief distortion: agents overweight outcomes whose objective likelihood has risen the most given recent news. In linear-Gaussian environments: E_t^theta[x_{t+1}] = E_t[x_{t+1}] + theta * (E_t[x_{t+1}] - E_{t-1}[x_{t+1}]).

front: How do diagnostic expectations explain corporate earnings forecast errors and return reversals?
back: Following a positive earnings surprise, analysts overreact by projecting excessive future growth (theta > 0). When future realizations inevitably regress to the mean, negative earnings surprises occur. Consequently, analyst forecast errors (Actual - Forecast) are negatively predicted by past earnings news, driving return reversals.

front: What is the rational risk explanation for cross-sectional anomaly factor premia (e.g. Fama & French 1993)?
back: Factor premia (such as the value premium HML or size premium SMB) represent compensation for bearing systematic, non-diversifiable macroeconomic distress risk or state-variable covariance that worsens investor marginal utility during bad economic states.

front: What is the behavioral mispricing explanation for cross-sectional anomalies?
back: Anomalies reflect persistent cognitive errors (extrapolation of past growth, overconfidence) and limits to arbitrage (short-sale constraints, idiosyncratic risk). Stocks with low book-to-market (growth) are systematically overpriced, while high book-to-market (value) stocks are underpriced, generating predictability unrelated to factor risk.

front: What was Daniel & Titman's (1997) characteristic vs covariance test?
back: By constructing portfolios that separated book-to-market characteristics from HML factor loadings, Daniel and Titman tested whether high book-to-market stocks with low HML beta earn high returns. They found the firm characteristic (book-to-market) drove returns, while factor covariance had no explanatory power once characteristic was controlled.

front: How do earnings announcement returns help distinguish between risk and mispricing?
back: If an anomaly reflects rational risk, excess returns should accrue smoothly across all trading days throughout the quarter. If an anomaly reflects mispricing correction, systematic abnormal returns will be concentrated in narrow windows around quarterly earnings announcements when objective information forces biased expectations to correct.

front: What is the 'short-leg asymmetry' observed in cross-sectional anomalies following high sentiment?
back: Because short-sale constraints and borrowing fees impede arbitrageurs from shorting overvalued stocks, mispricing is concentrated in overvalued assets. Following high sentiment, virtually the entire long-short anomaly spread is generated by dramatic underperformance of the short leg, while the long leg performs normally.

front: What does post-publication return decay (McLean & Pontiff 2016) imply about anomaly explanations?
back: McLean & Pontiff (2016) find academic anomaly returns attenuate by an average of 58% post-publication. If anomalies reflected rational compensation for systematic risk, publication would not diminish factor premia; return attenuation demonstrates that market participants learn of mispricings and arbitrage them down.
